newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's 96/97 surplus seen at HK$16 bln - A.Andersen.
newsitem.headline: HK's 96/97 surplus seen at HK$16 bln - A.Andersen.

text.p: Hong Kong is estimated to post a budget surplus of HK$16 billion for the 1996/97 fiscal year ending March 31, or 10 times the official estimate of HK$1.6 billion, Arthur Andersen said on Tuesday.
"It's mainly because of the healthy and active stock markets in the past few months," said partner Marcellus Wong who specialises in tax and business advisory services.
"Stamp duties collected have gone up. Property transactions and the economy have also improved," he said.
The firm estimates Hong Kong's financial reserves at HK$148.6 billion as of March 31, 1996 and HK$164.6 billion by March 31, 1997.
Its separate land reserve fund was also estimated at HK$141 billion when it is handed to the Special Administrative Region (SAR) government, which would run Hong Kong from July 1.
Hong Kong, a British colony of over 150 years, would revert to become an SAR under Chinese rule from midnight this June 1.
Despite its healthy finances, Hong Kong will need to revamp its tax regime and offer better terms to businesses if it wants to keep ahead of the competition, partners at the firm said.
Countries like Singapore, Taiwan and Malaysia have begun wooing investors recently through offering perks and Hong Kong would be left behind if it failed to catch up, said Becky Lai.
"I think regional coutries are using a lot of measures to catch up on the competitive edge of Hong Kong," Lai said.
"In the immediate term, it would be Singapore in terms of regional headquarters and financial centre," she said.
"In the long term, it would be Taiwan...in every aspect. Air, shipping, what we do, they will do. They are planning," Lai told reporters at a news conference.
The firm urged the Hong Kong government to consider reducing corporate tax rates by 1.5 percent from 16.5 percent now.

While corporate tax in Hong Kong was comparatively lower than those seen in the region - 26 percent in Singapore, 30 percent in Malaysia and Thailand and 35 in the Philippines - businesses are hit by "hidden" taxes like rents, Lai said.

"Although lost revenue is estimated at HK$3.75 billion per year, it would be compensated by increased investment," said fellow partner Wong, who added that the territory would also be bolstered by its healthy fiscal reserves.
The firm also urged a reduction in stamp duties on stock transactions, now at 0.3 percent in Hong Kong against 0.05 percent in Singapore and 0.1 percent in Malaysia and Thailand.
"The loss in revenue can be compensated by increase in revenues brought in by more investment in Hong Kong," Wong said.

Hong Kong also needed to build an international tax treaty network because the Commonwealth Tax Relief provision it now enjoys would be repealed after the territory reverts to Chinese rule, Wong said.
